metadata.title: The Sugarglass Debt
metadata.premise: In a storybook country curdled into nightmare, the village of Thistlewick still pays for a bargain its grandparents broke with the Godmother in the Wood. A party of outsiders is drawn in to settle the old wrong before the curse swallows what's left of the land.
metadata.narrationVoice: a wry, melancholic storybook narrator whose cheerful cadence keeps curdling into dread

contentLimits.note: The old wrong involves a childhood bargain broken decades ago; no harm to children is ever shown on-screen, only its lingering adult consequences.

beats.title: The Crooked Signpost
beats.prose: A signpost stands bent at the border of Thistlewick Vale, its painted letters weeping down the wood like candle wax. Three roads split from here: one into a huddled village, one into a wood gone the color of old bruises, one down toward a broken bridge where a toll was once collected.

options.label: Walk into the village of Thistlewick
Follow the crow-cries into the Hollow Wood
Investigate the ruined toll bridge

beats.title: Thistlewick Square
beats.prose: Shutters are nailed closed and the well in the square is capped with iron. A gaunt woman sweeping ash from her step tells you the mayor still keeps office, though grief has hollowed him like a gourd.

options.label: Seek out the weeping mayor
Head out to the Hollow Wood
Walk down to the toll bridge

beats.title: The Hollow Wood
beats.prose: The trees here have faces pressed into their bark, mouths open in permanent silent song. A wall of black briar rises ahead, and somewhere beyond it something sweet is burning.

options.label: Push on toward the briar wall
Turn back to the village
Cut east to the toll bridge

beats.title: The Toll Bridge Ruins
beats.prose: A stone bridge, half-collapsed, spans a ravine of black water. A rotted tollbooth still stands sentinel, its ledger-slot stuffed with claw marks. Something is nesting in the wreckage.

options.label: Search the ruins for records
Return to the village
Head into the Hollow Wood

beats.title: The Briar Wall
beats.prose: The briars are warm to the touch and hum a lullaby that makes your teeth ache. Somewhere beyond them, a grove waits that the wood itself seems desperate to hide.

options.label: Force a path through the thorns
Turn back to the village
Go to the toll bridge instead

beats.title: The Weeping Mayor
beats.prose: Mayor Corrin Vell sits behind a desk stacked with unpaid tithes to a power he won't name aloud. His eyes are red-rimmed but dry now, as if he has run out of the water for tears.

options.label: Ask about the old wrong done to the Godmother
Ask about the Godmother in the Wood
Try to end the curse without the Godmother's leave

beats.title: The Buried Ledger
beats.prose: Beneath rotten floorboards or brittle bridge-planks, you find a leather ledger. Generations ago, Thistlewick promised the Godmother a yearly toll of a child's laughter freely given. When the year came, the villagers hid their children away and paid her with counterfeit joy instead. She has been collecting the debt in curses ever since.

options.label: Seek out the mayor to explain the ledger
Head to the Godmother's grove
Confront the tollkeepers guarding the bridge

beats.title: The Grove's Edge
beats.prose: Sugarglass icicles hang from black branches, chiming like wind-bells over a ring of standing stones. Something in the grove watches without eyes, and demands you prove you belong here before you pass.

options.label: Solve the riddle of thorns
Offer the buried ledger as tribute
Force your way through the guardians

beats.title: The Grove's Watchers
beats.prose: Shapes peel off the standing stones like ink lifting from paper, and the grove goes cold as grave-dirt.

beats.title: The Tollkeepers
beats.prose: From the wreckage of the tollbooth spill goblins in patchwork coats, led by a scarred hobgoblin who still, absurdly, demands a toll before you may cross.

beats.title: The Godmother in the Wood
beats.prose: She is stitched together from storybook things: a crown of thorned sugar, a smile too wide, eyes like wells with no bottom. 'You have found my ledger,' she says, or perhaps only your bones hear it. 'Now. What will you pay me, that Thistlewick would not?'

options.label: Offer to pay the true toll yourselves
Demand she lift the curse without payment
Use the ledger's truth to strike a new bargain

beats.title: The Reckoning
beats.prose: The grove holds its breath. Whatever you chose to offer, the Godmother now waits to see it made real, and the vale itself seems to lean in to listen.

options.label: Accept the burden of the old debt
Shatter the bargain and unmake the curse
Seal the new bargain with the Godmother

beats.title: The Toll Paid
beats.prose: You give her what Thistlewick withheld: a true and willing joy, freely offered, taken from your own hearts rather than stolen from a child. The curse lifts from the vale like fog burning off at dawn, but something in each of you stays a little colder, a little quieter, for the rest of your days. Thistlewick sings again. You do not, quite, anymore.

beats.title: The Bargain Shattered
beats.prose: You refuse to pay her anything at all, and instead tear the old bargain out by its roots, ledger and grove and all. The Godmother's shriek unmakes the standing stones. The curse breaks, but so does whatever kept the vale's nightmares penned in one place — Thistlewick is free, and utterly unprotected, and the wood beyond it is stranger than ever. Freedom, it turns out, is its own kind of debt.

beats.title: A Fairer Bargain
beats.prose: Ledger in hand, you name the old lie for what it was, and the Godmother — who is nothing if not a creature of contracts — agrees to strike a new and honest bargain in its place. Thistlewick will pay a small, true, willingly-given toll each year, openly, forever. The vale wakes from its nightmare slowly, like a sleeper unsure the dream has really ended. You are the debt-holders now, and she will remember your names.

beats.title: The Curse Collects
beats.prose: You reached for the vale's oldest wound without her leave, or fell to what guards it, and the debt comes due on you instead. The sugarglass wood closes over the vale a little tighter, and Thistlewick's bells toll once, for strangers who almost helped, and did not.
